42026: Jesus' warnings against those who 'devour widows' houses' echo Micah's indictment of land-grabbing leaders.
42027: Matthew cites Micah 5:2 to show that the Messiah came from Bethlehem, David's town (Matt 2:6; compare John 7:42). Micah describes this ruler as a shepherd who will be 'great to the ends of the earth' and 'our peace' (Mic 5:4-5), language Christians apply to Jesus the good shepherd who 'is our peace' (John 10:11; Eph 2:14). The phrase about his origins 'from of old, from ancient days' (Mic 5:2) is read by many Christians as hinting at pre-existence; others, including Jewish interpreters, read it as pointing to David's ancient line. Jewish tradition (for example the Targum) also reads Mic 5:2 messianically, as the Messiah from David's house. Micah 7:20's promise of faithfulness to Abraham is echoed in Zechariah's song at John the Baptist's birth (Luke 1:72-73).
42028: Micah 6:8 as all religion needs, or as an impossible standard
42029: Micah 6:8 is quoted in two opposite ways: as a slogan meaning 'God just wants good people, not doctrine or worship', or, in some evangelical preaching, as a moral standard no one can meet, meant to drive people to grace.
42030: The verse answers a covenant lawsuit in which God first recalls what he has done: brought Israel out of Egypt, sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam, protected them from Balaam (Mic 6:3-5). Justice, hesed and humble walking are the fitting response of a rescued people to their rescuer, within the relationship. Scholars like Bruce Waltke and Francis Andersen stress this covenant framing; Jewish tradition reads it as the heart of Torah, not a replacement for it.
42031: Evangelical scholars agree the verse assumes grace already given, and that it is not a list of entrance requirements. Some (e.g. Waltke) also note that Israel's history shows how short people fall, so the verse naturally leads to Micah 7:18-20 and God's pardon. Both the moralist and the despair readings miss that grace and response belong together.
42032: Read in context, Micah 6:8 is neither a substitute for God nor a trap, but the shape of a life that answers God's saving love with justice and loyalty.
42033: Micah 5:2 only as a Christmas proof-text
42034: Micah 5:2 is known almost only as a Christmas prophecy proving that Jesus was the Messiah because he was born in Bethlehem.
42035: Micah's point is about the kind of king: in contrast to Jerusalem's corrupt rulers (Mic 3:1-3), God will raise a ruler from humble Bethlehem, David's origin, who shepherds in God's strength and brings peace after siege and exile. Andersen & Freedman and Hillers stress the anti-establishment contrast.
42036: Evangelical scholars (e.g. Waltke, Kenneth Barker) affirm that Matthew rightly sees Jesus as the fulfilment and that Jewish interpreters themselves read the verse of the Messiah (Matt 2:4-6 shows the priests did). They agree the birthplace matters less than what kind of shepherd-king he is.
42037: The fuller reading shows the Messiah as the answer to abusive power, not only a fulfilled prediction.
42038: Micah warned Jerusalem's elite that religious privilege would not save a city built on exploitation, and his warning moved Hezekiah to repent (Jer 26:19). After the exile, his promises gave a remnant hope of return, peace and a true king.
42039: Micah speaks to the misuse of power, the loss of homes and land to the powerful, and preachers who tell people what they want to hear. It also offers one of Scripture's clearest summaries of a faithful life and a closing picture of a God who throws sins into the sea.
42040: A poem of comfort for the victims of empire: the cruel city of Nineveh will fall, because the God who is slow to anger does not leave the guilty unpunished.
42041: A Judean prophet whose name means 'comfort'. His home town, Elkosh, is unknown; guesses range from Galilee (Capernaum, 'village of Nahum', is a later and doubtful link) to a site in Judah. He was a poet of unusual power, writing some of the most vivid battle verse in the Bible.
42042: The heading calls the book 'the oracle concerning Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite' (Nah 1:1), the only prophetic book called a 'book' (sefer) in its title, which suggests it was written, not just spoken.
42043: Nahum writes to comfort Judah (Nah 1:15). The exact location of Elkosh is unknown.
42044: Judah, living under Assyrian domination; the oracles are addressed rhetorically to Nineveh
42046: For over a century Assyria had deported, taxed and terrorised the nations, including Israel and Judah. Nahum announces that its capital will fall, as indeed it did in 612 BC.
42047: Ashurbanipal's army sacks Thebes (No-Amon) in Egypt, the event Nahum cites as a warning (Nah 3:8-10).
42048: Death of Ashurbanipal (approximate); the Assyrian empire begins to unravel in civil war.
42049: Nabopolassar becomes king of Babylon and leads its revolt against Assyria.
42050: Babylonians and Medes besiege and destroy Nineveh; the Babylonian Chronicle records its fall.
42051: The last Assyrian king loses Harran; Assyria disappears as a power.
42052:
In Nahum's lifetime Assyria was the greatest empire the world had yet seen. Its kings recorded their campaigns proudly: deportations of whole peoples, mounds of severed heads, captives flayed or impaled. Judah had survived Sennacherib's siege in 701 BC but stayed a vassal, paying tribute, under Manasseh. Nineveh, its capital, was enormous, with a city wall about twelve kilometres around, palaces, gardens and an aqueduct system. Its wealth came from plunder and tribute, which is why Nahum calls it 'the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder' (Nah 3:1).

Nahum mentions the fall of Thebes, Egypt's great city, to the Assyrians in 663 BC, so he wrote after that. Nineveh fell in 612 BC to a coalition of Babylonians and Medes, so he wrote before it, or at least before it was common knowledge. Most place him in the later 600s, when Assyria's decline after Ashurbanipal's death made its fall imaginable. The book's vivid descriptions of chariots, shields and opened gates (Nah 2:3-6) are poetry; some scholars link 'the river gates are opened' to a flood mentioned by later Greek writers, but the Babylonian Chronicle says nothing of a flood and others read the line figuratively.

After 612 BC Nineveh was never rebuilt as a capital. When the Greek historian Xenophon passed the site two centuries later, he did not even recognise it by name.
42054: A massa, or 'burden', is a prophetic judgment speech against a foreign power. Though aimed at Nineveh, it was heard by Judah as good news.
42056: Nahum opens with God marching in storm and earthquake, drying seas and melting mountains, the way older poems describe God leading Israel out of Egypt. It assures that God is stronger than any empire.
42058: Nahum 1:2-8 is a partial alphabetic acrostic: successive lines begin with successive Hebrew letters for about half the alphabet, a sign of careful, artful composition.
42060: A runner on the mountains brings word that the enemy is beaten, so Judah may again keep its feasts in peace. The same image appears in Isaiah for the return from exile.
42062: Chapter 3 mocks Nineveh as a sorceress-prostitute and its officials as locusts that fly away, a common ancient form of shaming a fallen enemy.
42063:
Nahum is not read as a haftarah in the regular synagogue cycle, but its opening creed has a deep place in Jewish theology. Nahum 1:2-3 restates God's self-description from Exodus 34:6-7 ('slow to anger... will by no means clear the guilty') but stresses its second half, while Jonah 4:2 stresses its first. Rabbinic and modern Jewish readers often pair the two: the same God who spared a repentant Nineveh in Jonah judges an unrepentant Nineveh in Nahum. Medieval Jewish commentators commonly explained the difference by saying that Nineveh's repentance in Jonah's day did not last, so the judgment once withheld finally came.

For a covenant people who had lost the northern tribes to Assyria, Nahum is not gloating but the vindication of God's justice: God is 'a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him' (Nah 1:7). The promise that Judah may 'keep your feasts, fulfil your vows' (Nah 1:15) shows the goal: freedom to worship and live under God rather than an emperor. The Dead Sea Scrolls include a commentary on Nahum (4QpNah, the *Pesher Nahum*), which applied its imagery to the community's own enemies, including the Hasmonean ruler who crucified his opponents, showing how Nahum became a lens for later tyranny.
42065: A hymn of God's power: slow to anger yet great in might, a refuge for those who trust him and an overwhelming flood to his foes.
42067: Oracles alternate: the yoke on Judah will be broken, Nineveh's line cut off; a herald announces peace.
42069: A vivid battle scene: red shields, racing chariots, opened gates, plunder carried off.
42071: Assyria, which hunted like a lion to feed its cubs, will itself be hunted.
42072: Nineveh's violence and lies are exposed; like Thebes, it will fall.
42074: Its defences crumble, its officials flee, and all who hear clap their hands, for who has not suffered its cruelty?
42092: Executing just retribution, the right of a lawful ruler, not private revenge; God does it, so his people need not.
42094: Zealous, protective of a covenant relationship; used of God's passion for his people and his own honour.
42096: A fortress and the act of taking shelter; God knows those who shelter in him.
42097: Wholeness and security; the herald's good news is that the oppressor is gone.
42098: Jonah shows God sparing a repentant Nineveh; Nahum shows him judging it once its cruelty returns. Both quote the Exodus 34 creed, from opposite sides.
42099: Isaiah also announces Assyria's downfall and uses the same 'beautiful feet' herald image for good news.
42100: Kings describes Assyria's conquest of Israel and siege of Jerusalem, the history Nahum answers.
42101: Paul applies the herald of good news to those who preach Christ, and tells believers to leave vengeance to God.
42102: Revelation's taunt over fallen Babylon, the city of luxury, sorcery and blood, closely parallels Nahum's song over Nineveh.
42103: Christians read Nahum's herald on the mountains 'who brings good news, who publishes peace' (Nah 1:15) through Paul, who applies the image to preachers of the gospel of Christ (Rom 10:15). The book's picture of God defeating an oppressive power that held his people captive is echoed in the New Testament's language of Christ disarming 'the rulers and authorities' (Col 2:15). At the same time Jesus forbids his followers personal vengeance (Matt 5:43-45), so Christians, like Jews, read Nahum as God's justice, not a permission for human revenge. Jewish readers see in Nahum the reassurance that no empire is permanent and that God remains the refuge of his covenant people.
42105: Many Christians either skip Nahum as embarrassing (a gleeful celebration of an enemy's destruction, out of step with 'love your enemies') or treat it as proof that the 'Old Testament God' was harsher than Jesus.
42106: Nahum was written for victims of one of history's most brutal empires. Julia O'Brien and J. J. M. Roberts note its hard edges but also its function: to assure the powerless that cruelty does not go unpunished and that God, not Judah, is the avenger. The book itself says God is 'slow to anger' and 'good, a stronghold' (Nah 1:3; Nah 1:7) and asks 'who has not felt your endless cruelty?' (Nah 3:19).
42107: Evangelical scholars such as O. Palmer Robertson and Tremper Longman argue that Nahum's God is the same as Jesus' God, who also warns of judgment (Matt 23:33-36), and that Revelation celebrates the fall of oppressive 'Babylon' in similar terms. They agree that Nahum's voice must be balanced by Jonah's, but defend divine justice as good news for the oppressed. Scholars with ethical reservations (e.g. O'Brien) still accept that the book speaks from the underside of empire.
42108: Seeing Nahum as justice for the oppressed helps readers hear it as hope, not hatred, and keeps the Bible's witness on mercy and justice together.
42109: For Judah under the Assyrian boot, Nahum said that the empire was not eternal, that God had seen its crimes, and that they would again be free to keep their feasts.
42110: Nahum gives words to people suffering under abusive power, assuring them that God is a refuge and that tyranny will not last. It also warns any strong nation, church or person that violence and exploitation carry their own judgment.
42111: A prophet argues with God about injustice and about God using cruel Babylon, waits for an answer, and ends singing that he will rejoice in God even if every crop fails.
42113: A Judean prophet in Jerusalem in the late 600s BC. Unusually, he is called 'the prophet' (ha-navi) in the heading, and the final psalm carries musical directions, which has led some to think he served among the temple singers.
42114: The headings (Hab 1:1; Hab 3:1). A later legend in the Greek additions to Daniel (*Bel and the Dragon*) has an angel carry Habakkuk to Babylon to feed Daniel in the lions' den; this is tradition, not history.
42115: The setting is Judah facing the rise of Babylon, probably under King Jehoiakim.
42116: The faithful in Judah who were troubled by injustice at home and terror abroad
42117: After Josiah's reforms collapsed, Jehoiakim's Judah was full of violence and bent justice. Then the Babylonians (Chaldeans) defeated Egypt and Assyria and swept into the region, raising a harder question: how can a good God use a worse nation to judge his own?
42118: King Josiah is killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Neco; Jehoiakim is placed on the throne.
42119: Nebuchadnezzar defeats Egypt at Carchemish and becomes king of Babylon; Judah becomes a Babylonian vassal.
42120: A drawn battle between Babylon and Egypt encourages Jehoiakim to rebel.
42121: Nebuchadnezzar captures Jerusalem and deports King Jehoiachin and leading citizens.
42122:
Habakkuk lived through whiplash. Josiah's reforms of the 620s had raised hopes of renewal, but Josiah died in battle in 609 BC and his son Jehoiakim reversed much of it, building a lavish palace with unpaid labour (Jer 22:13-17). Inside Judah, Habakkuk sees 'violence', 'strife' and a law that is 'paralysed' (Hab 1:2-4).

Abroad, the Neo-Babylonian empire was rising fast. The Babylonians, whom the Bible calls Chaldeans after their tribal origins in southern Mesopotamia, joined the Medes to destroy Nineveh in 612 BC and then crushed Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC. Habakkuk describes their cavalry as faster than leopards and their army as a fishing net that sweeps up nations (Hab 1:8; Hab 1:14-17). God tells him he is raising them up to judge Judah, which only deepens the prophet's distress.

The book is shaped as a dialogue: two complaints and two answers, a series of five 'woes' against the oppressor, and a closing psalm. Its central line, 'the righteous shall live by his faith (or faithfulness)' (Hab 2:4), became one of the most quoted OT verses in the New Testament and in later Christian theology.
42124: Israel's faith allowed honest protest to God: 'How long, O LORD?' Habakkuk argues in the tradition of the lament psalms, not as an unbeliever but as a covenant partner.
42125: A sentry on the walls watched for messengers. Habakkuk stations himself to wait for God's reply, a picture of patient, alert faith.
42127: God tells him to write the vision on tablets so that 'he may run who reads it', probably so a herald can carry the message, and because its fulfilment will come at the appointed time.
42129: 'Woe' (hoy) was a funeral cry. Five woes against the oppressor condemn plunder, unjust gain, bloodshed, humiliating others and idolatry.
42131: Musical terms in Habakkuk 3, as in the Psalms. They show the prayer was sung in worship; their exact meaning is uncertain.
42133: A dramatic appearance of God, here coming from Teman and Mount Paran in the south as at Sinai, shaking the earth and splitting rivers, recalling the exodus and conquest.
42134:
Habakkuk 2:20 through 3:19 is the haftarah for the second day of Shavuot, the festival of the giving of the Torah. Its vision of God coming from Teman and Paran with brilliance and shaking the mountains is read as a poetic memory of the revelation at Sinai. The Talmud (*Makkot* 24a) says that Habakkuk reduced all the commandments to one principle: 'the righteous shall live by his faith (emunah)' (Hab 2:4). In Hebrew emunah means steady trustworthiness and faithful trust together: the person who stays loyal to God when everything seems to contradict his promises.

The Dead Sea Scrolls include a running commentary on Habakkuk 1-2, the *Pesher Habakkuk* (1QpHab), one of the first scrolls found. It reads the Chaldeans as the 'Kittim' (probably the Romans) and applies Hab 2:4 to those in Judah who keep the Torah and stay faithful to the community's 'Teacher of Righteousness', showing that already before Paul the verse was a focus for questions about who will be saved in the end time. For Jewish readers today, Habakkuk models a faith that argues with God from inside the covenant and then chooses to trust him: 'though the fig tree does not blossom... yet I will rejoice in the LORD' (Hab 3:17-18).
42136: Habakkuk complains that violence fills Judah and God seems not to act.
42138: God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans, swift and ruthless, to judge Judah.
42140: How can a holy God use the wicked to swallow those more righteous? Habakkuk climbs his watchtower to wait.
42141: Write the vision; live by faith
42142: The answer will surely come; the proud will fall, but the righteous will live by faithfulness.
42144: The plunderer will be plundered; the earth will be filled with the knowledge of God's glory; let all the earth be silent.
42146: Habakkuk recalls God marching out to save his people as in the exodus.
42148: Though harvests fail and flocks vanish, he will rejoice in the God of his salvation.
42168: Firmness, reliability, steady trust; the righteous person holds on to God and stays loyal through the crisis.
42170: Brutal wrongdoing; Habakkuk's first complaint and the charge against Babylon.
42171: A revelation from God, to be written down and awaited.
42172: To exult and dance for joy; the book's last word on God despite loss.
42173: Paul quotes Hab 2:4 as the theme text for the gospel: the righteous will live by faith.
42174: Paul uses Hab 2:4 to argue that justification comes by faith, not by the works of the law.
42175: Hebrews quotes Hab 2:3-4 (Greek) to urge persecuted believers to endure and not shrink back.
42176: Paul warns the synagogue in Pisidian Antioch with Hab 1:5: 'Look, you scoffers... I am doing a work you would not believe.'
42177: Habakkuk's complaint and closing song follow the shape of the lament psalms, moving from protest to trust.
42178: The earth 'filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD' echoes Isaiah's vision of the messianic age.
42179: Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted three times in the New Testament (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11; Heb 10:38), each time to show how God's people live in the time between promise and fulfilment: by trusting God's faithfulness revealed in Jesus. Some scholars (e.g. Richard Hays, Douglas Campbell) argue that Paul hears 'the righteous one' as Jesus himself, the faithful one whose faithfulness brings life; others (e.g. Douglas Moo) hold it means the believer who trusts. Hebrews, following the Greek text, applies 'the coming one will come and will not delay' to Christ's return (Heb 10:37). Jewish readers do not read a messianic figure in the verse; they hear a call to steadfast covenant loyalty under pressure. Both readings meet in Habakkuk's closing confession that joy in God does not depend on circumstances.
42180: 'The righteous shall live by faith': faith alone, or faithfulness?
42181: Since Luther, Habakkuk 2:4 is often read through Romans as the classic proof of justification by faith alone: individuals are declared right with God by believing, not by doing anything.
42182: In Habakkuk, emunah means faithfulness and steady trust, the loyalty of a covenant member who keeps holding on to God during invasion and injustice while the proud collapse. Scholars like Francis Andersen, J. J. M. Roberts and, on the Pauline side, N. T. Wright and Matthew Bates (with his stress on pistis as 'allegiance') argue that Paul's use keeps this sense of loyal trust, not a bare mental assent.
42183: Reformed and evangelical scholars such as Douglas Moo, Thomas Schreiner and O. Palmer Robertson reply that trusting God is not a work and that Paul rightly draws out the verse's contrast between the proud, self-reliant person and the one who depends on God. They agree emunah includes perseverance but argue that it is God's faithfulness, received by trust, that gives life. Many on both sides now agree that 'faith' and 'faithfulness' are not opposites: trust that endures is the point.
42184: Hearing Habakkuk's own context keeps 'faith' from shrinking to a one-time decision and shows it as the enduring trust that carries God's people through crisis.
42185: 'Write the vision and make it plain' (Hab 2:2) as goal-setting
42186: Hab 2:2 is widely used for personal vision statements, vision boards, church strategic plans or business goals: write down your dream and God will bring it to pass.
42187: The 'vision' is God's revelation to Habakkuk about judgment on Babylon and the survival of the faithful. It is written down so a herald can carry it and so that people can wait for God's appointed time (Hab 2:3). It is God's plan, not the reader's.
42188: Some pastors argue that the principle of clearly communicating a God-given direction is legitimate by analogy. Evangelical commentators (e.g. Robertson, Bruckner) generally agree the analogy is loose and warn against attaching the promise 'it will surely come' to human plans.
42189: Applied to our own dreams, the verse can become a promise God never made; read in context it teaches patient trust in God's timing for his justice.
42190: For faithful Judeans facing invasion, Habakkuk gave permission to question God honestly and showed a way through: wait, trust God's justice, stay faithful, and find joy in God when everything else is stripped away.
42191: Habakkuk is a guide for anyone who has asked why God allows injustice or why things get worse after prayer. It models honest complaint, patient waiting and a joy in God that does not depend on harvests, health or success.
42192: Zephaniah warns complacent Jerusalem of a terrifying Day of the LORD that will sweep the whole earth, then pictures a humble remnant over whom God sings for joy.
42194: A Jerusalem prophet with a four-generation pedigree ending in 'Hezekiah' (Zeph 1:1), probably King Hezekiah, which would make him a distant cousin of King Josiah. His father's name, Cushi, has prompted the suggestion of African (Cushite) ancestry; this is possible but uncertain.
42195: The heading dates him to Josiah's reign. His intimate knowledge of Jerusalem's districts (the Fish Gate, the Second Quarter, the Mortar) suggests he lived in the city.
42196: He names city quarters and markets (Zeph 1:10-11).
42197: Jerusalem's officials, royal household, priests and merchants
42198: After the long reign of Manasseh, Jerusalem mixed the worship of the LORD with Baal, the 'host of heaven' and Milcom, adopted foreign fashions, and assumed God would do 'neither good nor ill'. Josiah's reform had not yet begun or was just beginning.
42199: Josiah becomes king of Judah at age eight after his father Amon is assassinated.
42200: Ashurbanipal dies (approximate); Assyria's grip on the west loosens.
